title: So for Strang, in conversion and works of grace man keeps only essential freedom, not indifference
source_text: XVI. Proinde secundum hujus viri doctrinam, quanquam homo in pluribus quae in hac vita degens agit, illa libertate gaudeat quae sita est in potestate ad opposita se determinandi; plurium tamen aliorum respectu quae sunt absolute Dei decreto praedefinita, libertatem eam non retinet, sed eam solum quae in eo sita est quod homo libens agit, & ex rationis propriae judicio. Quod praecipue locum habere putat in conversione hominis ad Deum & operibus gratiae. Nam, inquit, citra praedeterminationem Dei non potest homo converti, non potest pie agere; & posita praedeterminatione gratiae, non potest non converti, non potest non pie agere. Proinde in illis operibus etsi agnoscamus manere libertatem, quae voluntati est essentialis, tamen libertatem in strictiore isto sensu usurpatam illic locum habere negamus.
pass_a_gloss: XVI. Therefore according to the doctrine of this man, although man in most things which he does living in this life, enjoys that freedom which is placed in the power of determining himself to opposites; yet in respect of many others which are absolutely predefined by God's decree, he does not retain that freedom, but that only which is placed in this that man acts willingly, and from the judgement of his own reason. Which he thinks has place especially in the conversion of man to God and in works of grace. For, he says, without the predetermination of God man cannot be converted, cannot act piously; and the predetermination of grace being posited, he cannot not be converted, cannot not act piously. Therefore in those works although we acknowledge that the freedom remains, which is essential to the will, yet we deny that freedom used in that stricter sense has place there.
pass_b_english: On this man's teaching, then, in most of what he does in this life man enjoys the freedom that consists in the power to determine himself to either of two opposites. But with respect to many other acts that are absolutely predefined by God's decree he does not keep that freedom, only the freedom that consists in acting willingly and by the judgement of his own reason.

He thinks this holds above all in man's conversion to God and in the works of grace. 'Without God's predetermination,' he says, 'a man cannot be converted and cannot act piously; and once the predetermination of grace is in place, he cannot fail to be converted and cannot fail to act piously. So although we acknowledge that the freedom essential to the will remains in those works, we deny that freedom in the stricter sense has any place there.'
